lesson.title: Planning and tool use with language models
lesson.subtitle: Search, ReAct and tool calls

video.title: Planning and tool use with language models: Search, ReAct and tool calls
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A student's assistant agent is asked for a free room on Tuesday. It confidently names a room that does not exist. It never called the booking tool it had. Why not?

scenes.on_screen_text: Planning and tool use with language models
scenes.narration: Today: how classical planners search for action sequences, how language-model agents interleave reasoning with tool calls, and how to teach students to build and debug both.
Planning finds a sequence of actions that takes the world from a start state to a goal. Each action has preconditions and effects. A planner searches this space instead of guessing.
A star search expands the node with the lowest cost so far plus estimated cost to go. If the estimate never overestimates, the plan it finds is optimal. Students can trace it by hand on a small map.
A ReAct agent writes a thought, calls a tool, and reads the observation before its next step. Here it checks the booking system before answering. The answer is grounded in what the tool returned.

A language model may answer from memory instead of calling a tool, especially if the tool's description is vague. Clear tool descriptions, explicit instructions, and checking every answer against a tool result all reduce this.

Students now meet agents through language models and skip classical planning. Teach both. Search gives guarantees and a vocabulary of states and goals. Language-model agents give flexibility, and the classical ideas explain their failures.
Quick check! A star uses a heuristic that sometimes overestimates the remaining cost. Is the plan it finds guaranteed to be optimal?
No. Optimality needs an admissible heuristic, one that never overestimates. With an overestimate, A star may skip the best path.
In the app, open the Plan in steps lab. Pick a goal that needs two tools, guess the plan, run it, and see what Darsi Tiny does on Saturday, when the first step fails.
Your turn. Which change most directly stops the agent from inventing a room?
Requiring the answer to come from a tool result, and checking it. Remember: planners search with heuristics, ReAct interleaves thought with tools, and answers should be grounded in observations.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it in your next lecture
scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: trace A star on a six-node campus map on the board. Then show a ReAct transcript with one missing tool call. Pairs find the step where the agent should have acted.
